newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Kohl winds up Czech visit with Havel meeting.
newsitem.headline: Kohl winds up Czech visit with Havel meeting.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl wound up a landmark visit to the Czech Republic on Wednesday by paying his respects at the grave of a dissident cardinal and lunching with President Vaclav Havel.
Kohl, who signed a post-war reconciliation accord with the Czech Republic on Tuesday, visited the grave of Frantisek Tomasek who for 40 years championed religious freedom in communist Czechoslovakia.
He held talks with Tomasek's successor, Cardinal Miloslav Vlk and had a private lunch with Havel. He was flying out later in the day.

"I understand this meeting, which was held at the initiative of the German side, as acknowledgement of what the church has done in the past six years in Czech-German relations," Vlk said, adding that the talks had focused mainly on Kohl's vision of European unification.
Kohl, on his first visit to Prague since he attended Tomasek's funeral in 1992, signed the declaration with Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus.
He said Germany wanted to forgive and be forgiven, and pledged German support for Czech membership of the European Union and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
In the accord, Bonn expresses sorrow for the 1938-45 Nazi occupation of Czech land and Prague voiced its regret at Czech brutality in the post-war expulsion of 2.5 million Germans.

"In his speech (Kohl) said all the right things and I think he scored very well with both the defenders of the declaration and its opponents," said Jiri Pehe, head of research at Prague's Open Media research institute.

However the accord remains controversial in both countries. It provides no compensation for the expelled Germans' confiscated property and Kohl said property issues remained open. This point was highlighted in many Czech newspapers.

"Opening (property questions) is restricted only by the agreement of the states not to burden relations with political and legal questions from the past. But this does not forbid individuals or lobby groups from pushing their claims," the Mlada Fronta Dnes daily said.
Czech communists and far-right Republicans also oppose the declaration, insisting it means a loss of Czech sovereignty.

The Czech Republic, along with Poland and Hungary, is seen as a leading candidate to join both the EU and NATO. However, many Czechs are wary about joining new alliances after the years of Nazi occupation and subsequent Soviet domination.
The declaration, drawn up after two years of delicate negotiations, still needs the approval of both parliaments.
Klaus, who hopes the declaration will give fresh impetus to Czech EU and NATO membership plans, called in his speech on Tuesday for both assemblies to back the accord.
The main Czech opposition party, the Social Democrats, are split over the issue and their support is uncertain.
"It will get through parliament but it will be close. The Social Democrats will try to play a game," said Pehe.
Kohl's support on Europe follows similar sentiments from French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, who said in Prague last week that the Czechs could join the EU in the year 2000.
"That will make the discussion here more lively," he said.
The European Commission said on Wednesday, however, that the EU was unlikely to admit new members before 2002.
